title: Break-even analysis with a worked calculation for Mobile massage
audience: Mobile massage therapists who set prices or plan monthly income from a vehicle, a phone and a session diary.
learningOutcomes: Classify the costs of a mobile massage business as fixed or variable
Calculate monthly break-even revenue and the number of sessions it needs
Explain why conflicting break-even figures must be reconciled before any of them is used

instruction.heading: What break-even means
instruction.body: Break-even revenue is the amount of sales that covers all costs exactly, so profit is zero. Below that level the business loses money. Above it, each further dollar of sales adds to profit. For a mobile massage therapist, the figure shows how many sessions a month must be booked before the vehicle, insurance and equipment are paid for. It is a planning tool, and its answer is only as good as the costs and percentages that go into it.

instruction.heading: Split costs into fixed and variable
instruction.body: Fixed costs do not change with the number of sessions in a month. For a mobile massage business they include vehicle finance or lease repayments, registration, public liability insurance, phone and booking software, and any council or state fee that applies to the work, once you have confirmed it. Variable costs move with each session. They include oils and products used on the client, linen or its laundering, disposable items, payment fees charged on each sale, and fuel for the travel to each client. ANZ defines fixed costs as those that stay the same whatever the volume of work and variable costs as those that move with it, and warns that costs must be covered to avoid operating at a loss. Express variable cost as a share of sales: divide the variable cost in a period by the sales in the same period. Check that share across at least three months before you rely on it, because one unusual month can mislead.

instruction.heading: The formula
instruction.body: Break-even revenue equals fixed costs divided by one minus the variable cost percentage. The quantity one minus the variable percentage is the contribution margin, which is the share of each dollar of sales that is left to cover fixed costs. Use the percentage as a decimal, so 10 per cent becomes 0.10. Xero Australia states the same method: the contribution margin is the selling price minus the variable cost, the ratio is the margin divided by the price, and break-even revenue is fixed costs divided by that ratio (glossary, 23 July 2026).

instruction.heading: Work the calculation in order
instruction.body: Write the inputs first, each with its source and date. Compute the contribution margin. Divide the fixed costs by it. Convert the result into a number of sessions at your average price, and round up to whole sessions, because a part session does not cover costs on its own. The figures in this lesson are illustrative only and are not market data. The method is the check: divide fixed costs by the contribution margin, then test the result against inputs you can source from your own bank and booking records.

instruction.heading: Reconcile before you use any figure
instruction.body: When two figures disagree, go back to the inputs. Confirm that each fixed cost is a monthly amount and not an annual one, such as a yearly insurance premium or a yearly registration fee. Confirm that the variable percentage is a share of sales and not of cost. Confirm that the output is revenue and not profit. Then write down the reconciled figure with its inputs and drop the others. A figure that cannot be checked should not be used to set prices.

procedure: List every monthly cost and label each one fixed or variable.
Work out variable cost as a percentage of sales for the same period, and check it across at least three months.
Calculate one minus the variable percentage to find the contribution margin.
Divide monthly fixed costs by the contribution margin to get break-even revenue.
Divide break-even revenue by your average session price to get the number of sessions needed each month, rounded up.
Compare any other break-even figure with your result, reconcile the inputs, and keep only the reconciled figure.

workedExamples.situation: A mobile massage therapist (illustrative figures, not market data) has fixed costs of $2,200 AUD a month for the vehicle, insurance, equipment and booking software. Variable costs are 10 per cent of sales, and the average session price is $100 AUD.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: How many sessions must the business complete each month to break even, and what should it check before setting prices?
workedExamples.reasoning: The contribution margin is 1 minus 0.10, which is 0.90. Break-even revenue is $2,200 AUD divided by 0.90, which is $2,444.44 AUD a month. Each session contributes $100 AUD multiplied by 0.90, which is $90.00 AUD. At $100 AUD a session, $2,444.44 AUD is 24.44 sessions, so 25 sessions are needed. Before setting prices, check that the 10 per cent includes oils, linen and payment fees, that the $2,200 AUD is a monthly figure, and that $100 AUD is the average price charged after any discounts.

equipmentAndPpe: Cost list for the last three months, marked fixed or variable

commonErrors.error: Mixing monthly and annual figures, such as a yearly insurance premium or registration fee
commonErrors.prevention: Convert every cost to the same period before dividing, and label each input with its period.

commonErrors.error: Using variable cost as a share of cost instead of a share of sales
commonErrors.prevention: Divide variable cost by sales for the same period, and write the denominator beside the percentage.

commonErrors.error: Copying a break-even figure from another therapist without its inputs
commonErrors.prevention: Recalculate from your own inputs and record the source and date of each input before using the result.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Business planning only. This lesson gives no tax or accounting advice. Vehicle running costs and GST depend on your circumstances. Check the ATO’s current vehicle rate yourself, and check the tax treatment of costs with a registered tax agent.

This lesson does not grant any licence, registration or authority. Massage registration rules were not verified for most states and territories, so do not enter a registration fee as a fixed cost until you have confirmed that it applies to your work.

qualityStandard: Every break-even figure shows its fixed costs, variable percentage, period and source.
Two figures that disagree are reconciled before either one is used in a plan or a price.
documentationEvidence: Cost list split into fixed and variable, with source and date
Reconciliation note wherever two figures disagree
summary: Break-even revenue is fixed costs divided by one minus the variable cost percentage.
Use one period throughout the calculation.
Recalculate from your own inputs. Do not copy another therapist’s break-even figure.

knowledgeChecks.question: Break-even revenue is calculated as:
options: Fixed costs divided by (1 minus the variable cost percentage)
Fixed costs multiplied by the variable cost percentage
Sales minus fixed costs, shown as a percentage of the cost

knowledgeChecks.question: Fixed costs are $2,200 AUD a month and variable costs are 10% of sales. What is the monthly break-even revenue?
Two sources give different break-even figures for the same business. What is the right response?
options: Use the larger figure to be safe and ignore the smaller figure entirely
Recalculate from your own costs and check each source's inputs before using any figure
Average the two figures together and quote the result to the client today
Use the price list alone and skip the break-even check and rely on the owner's gut feel
